ego.name: Lina Bo Bardi
ego.summary: Lina Bo Bardi was an Italian-born Brazilian modernist architect, designer, and editor whose work connected modern construction with Brazilian vernacular culture and public life. Her major projects include the São Paulo Museum of Art, the Glass House, Solar do Unhão, and SESC Pompéia.

connections.relationship_description: Bo Bardi's mother. Giovanna and Enrico Bo raised Lina in Rome before the birth of her younger daughter, Graziella.
Her husband and cultural partner from their 1946 marriage until Bo Bardi's death. In Brazil, they worked on MASP, founded Habitat, and lived in Casa de Vidro.
connections.notes: Their marriage was also a sustained cultural and professional partnership lasting until Bo Bardi's death.

connections.relationship_description: Bo Bardi worked with Pagani at Studio Bo e Pagani in Milan after graduating in 1939; they also documented war-damaged Italy for Domus in 1945 and helped establish A – Attualità, Architettura, Abitazione, Arte.
connections.notes: Their connection spanned architectural practice, postwar documentation, and editorial work.

connections.relationship_description: Fellow Italian immigrant Palanti worked with Bo Bardi at Studio d’Arte Palma and collaborated with her on the 1950 redesign of MASP's galleries in the Diários Associados building.
connections.notes: Their gallery redesign replaced Beaux-Arts display conventions with an avant-garde exhibition language.

connections.relationship_description: Bo Bardi's father. He did not fully support her decision to become an architect, and his adventurous, anarchist character influenced her early graphic sensibility.
connections.notes: The article identifies him as Lina's father and links his character to her representational style.

connections.relationship_description: Bo Bardi's younger sister; they were the two daughters of Enrico and Giovanna Bo.
Bo Bardi collaborated with Ponti as an architect and designer on the magazine Lo Stile – nella casa e nell’arredamento until 1943.
connections.notes: This Milan editorial work placed her within Italy's influential architecture and design press.

connections.relationship_description: Photographer Patellani traveled with Bo Bardi and Carlo Pagani on Domus's 1945 assignment to document and assess destruction across postwar Italy.
Bo Bardi, Zevi, and Carlo Pagani established the Milan weekly A – Attualità, Architettura, Abitazione, Arte, also known as A Cultura della Vita, after World War II.
connections.notes: The magazine joined architectural debate to the wider task of Italy's physical and moral reconstruction.

connections.relationship_description: Chateaubriand's creation of MASP with Pietro Maria Bardi enabled Bo Bardi to design the museum's first galleries in 1947 and later its landmark new building on Avenida Paulista.
connections.notes: Their connection centered on MASP, whose early premises occupied the headquarters of his media group.

connections.relationship_description: Bo Bardi collaborated with theater director Gonçalves on the 1959 Bahia exhibition at Ibirapuera, bringing together art, crafts, music, and images from Bahia for the V São Paulo Biennial.
connections.notes: The exhibition marked a transition toward her later experimental museum-display methods.

connections.relationship_description: Bo Bardi collaborated on Milano Sera while the newspaper was directed by Vittorini.
Piacentini Cirell worked alongside Bo Bardi at Studio d’Arte Palma, where she was responsible for the antiquarian section.

category_summaries.summary: Bo Bardi's family begins in Rome with Enrico, Giovanna, and her younger sister Graziella. Her 1946 marriage to Pietro Maria Bardi joins personal life to a shared Brazilian cultural practice. They leave Italy together, live in Casa de Vidro, and work through museums and publishing.

Bo Bardi's professional circle grows from Milan architecture and publishing into Brazil's museum and design institutions. Carlo Pagani, Giò Ponti, Federico Patellani, Bruno Zevi, and Elio Vittorini connect her to wartime and postwar editorial work in Italy. In São Paulo, MASP, Studio d’Arte Palma, and Habitat give her places to design exhibitions, publish, and work with art in public life.

In 1959, Bo Bardi and Martim Gonçalves bring the Bahia exhibition to the São Paulo Biennial. Their work joins exhibition design with artworks, crafts, music, and photographs from Bahia. It extends her architectural work into theater and visual culture.
